title: Markets Aren’t Random- The Drivers Behind Trend Formation - Systematic Investor - Ep.371

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/Markets Aren’t Random- The Drivers Behind Trend Formation - Systematic Investor - Ep.371.docx

speakers: Rich (Richard Brennan, Australian trend follower, 'outlier hunter')
summary:
Systematic Investor 371 (Nov 2025): Rich argues markets are reflexive, non-ergodic, fractal systems where trends arise from reinforcing feedback across time scales; Gaussian statistics fail.
Approach: ensembles of behaviorally orthogonal trend systems, survival-first closed-balance position sizing; Niels defends dynamic (volatility-based) sizing.
Conclusions: process over prediction, avoid ruin, low volatility is latent risk; AI will shorten prediction horizons, favouring trend.

completeness_estimate: 0.75 - first reader caught Rich's core framework (impact, reflexivity, non-ergodicity, fractals, closed-balance sizing, Niels' rebuttals); missed secondary mechanisms (adaptive liquidity, reversal mechanics, multi-scale cascade example, directional vs directionless volatility), several caveats/disagreement details, market-view items (energies, oil, dip-buying) and had one speaker error.

claims.speaker: Rich
claims.quote: You want rules, systematic processes. And you want data to be your guide, not your emotions to be your guide
claims.claim: Financial markets are not an environment humans evolved in, so rules-based left-brain processes (and AI) beat discretionary emotion, which constrains rule-following (e.g. fear when volatility rises).

claims.speaker: Rich
claims.quote: prediction in these markets is like prediction in the weather. It's ephemeral. It's got a very short range
claims.claim: Prediction horizon in markets is short, like weather, because of reflexivity; AI adoption will compress prediction horizons further, defeating itself and favouring trends from structure.

claims.speaker: Niels
claims.quote: gold if people don't follow this um has had it [clears throat] had had its biggest price drop on Tuesday I think it was in over a decade
claims.claim: Gold fell over 6% in a day (biggest drop in over a decade), silver and platinum more, palladium -16% in two days: precious metals volatility exploded, with implications for position sizing.

claims.speaker: Niels
claims.quote: electricity is now the core or input to growth
claims.claim: Quoting Saxo's former chief strategist: electricity is the successor to oil as the core input to growth; shortage of power, cooling and grid raises inflation and stalls productivity.

claims.speaker: Niels
claims.quote: Equities continue to be fairly well uh behaved from a trend following perspective
claims.claim: Late October 2025 trend environment: constructive, with metals correcting but trending, equities well-behaved, soft commodities (sugar, coffee, cotton) a new return source, energies and currencies range-bound.

claims.speaker: Rich
claims.quote: I think it's a very robust environment for trend following
claims.claim: Rich is bullish on trend following after a difficult first six months of 2025 with policy whipsaw.

claims.speaker: Rich
claims.quote: the events we saw post GFC up
claims.claim: Post-GFC to 2018 was the anomaly for trend; current decoupled, less coordinated central-bank environment is 'trend heaven', as long as everyday policy changes do not cause whipsaw ('death by a thousand cuts').

claims.speaker: Rich
claims.quote: what was perceived as calm was actually compression
claims.claim: QE and central bank coordination suppressed trends (compression, buy-the-dip) and stored energy released from 2020 like an avalanche; risk never went away.

claims.speaker: Rich
claims.quote: the stability of inflation how much that really impacts uh the markets we trade
claims.claim: The stability of inflation (not only its level) strongly shapes trending opportunities; central banks succeeded in keeping inflation stable, producing compression.

correction.issue: Wrong speaker: the points that central banks succeeded in keeping inflation low and stable, and that the stability (not just level) of inflation drives the markets trend followers trade, are made by Niels (Rich only interjects 'kicked the can down low with compression').
correction.fix: Niels: the stability of inflation, not just its level, strongly affects the markets trend followers trade; central banks succeeded in keeping inflation low and stable, which Rich links to the compression period.

claims.speaker: Niels
claims.quote: the trend barometer yesterday finished at 52
claims.claim: Trend barometer at 52, BTOP50 +2.12% in October (YTD +2.58%), SG CTA +2.35% (YTD -0.4%), SG Trend +2.85% (YTD +0.53%), MSCI World +18.3% YTD, US aggregate bond +9.8%, S&P 500 TR +15.08%.

claims.speaker: Rich
claims.quote: most people think price moves because information is revealed but markets move because impact is applied
claims.claim: Price moves because of trade impact (supply and demand changes), not information; each order reshapes conditions for the next, so reflexivity arises.

claims.speaker: Rich
claims.quote: prices therefore no longer just reflect information. They therefore create it through this feedback
claims.claim: Reflexive feedback: traders observe price, update models and act again; markets need only participants whose behavior feeds back, and evolve by interaction not equilibrium.

claims.speaker: Rich
claims.quote: impact grows with a square root of trade size
claims.claim: Market impact is sublinear (square-root law, Bouchaud): doubling order size raises impact only ~40%; small trades vanish in noise, but aligned small trades compound feedback and volatility clusters.

claims.speaker: Rich
claims.quote: this is what destroys erodicity in these markets and replaces it with path dependence
claims.claim: Market events are conditional (each changes probability of the next), so markets are path dependent and non-ergodic; ensemble statistics do not describe an individual wealth path (Ole Peters).

claims.speaker: Rich
claims.quote: the expectancy equation is what we call an erotic statistic
claims.claim: The expectancy equation ignores sequence of events and so is an ergodic statistic that misleads in markets.

claims.speaker: Rich
claims.quote: There's a lower finite bound and there is an open-ended bound
claims.claim: Wealth paths have a lower bound of zero (ruin) and compounding, making them non-ergodic; Gaussian-based tools (Markowitz, Sharpe, standard deviation, expectancy, risk of ruin) break down.

claims.speaker: Rich
claims.quote: a Gaussian distribution says that a five standard sigma event should occur every 170,000 years
claims.claim: The S&P 500 futures had 32 five-sigma events in 30 years versus one per 170,000 years under Gaussian; all liquid markets show fat tails, consistent with power laws and fractal behavior (Mandelbrot).
claims.indicator: five-sigma events; Hurst exponent; tail decay

claims.speaker: Rich
claims.quote: captured by things like the hertz exponent
claims.claim: Market memory is better measured with the Hurst exponent and tail properties than Gaussian tools.

claims.speaker: Rich
claims.quote: low volatility regimes I actually view as high latent risk events
claims.claim: Low volatility is latent compressed risk, like a sponge, awaiting a tipping point; volatility is not risk, and standard volatility measures cannot define risk.

claims.speaker: Rich
claims.quote: I refer to them as deterministic um unpredictable systems
claims.claim: Markets resemble weather: deterministic but unpredictable beyond a short horizon, interacting agents with no central governor produce periods of order and sudden large events.

claims.speaker: Rich
claims.quote: The same way as I think our systems need to be engineered to not be brittle, not be overoptimized, not be not be overfit
claims.claim: Build systems like an engineer designs a bridge: robust, resilient, not overfit or over-optimized rather than relying on Gaussian statistical protection.

claims.speaker: Rich
claims.quote: in fractal systems, you can never get rid of the structure
claims.claim: Fractal structure persists across scales: noise at high resolution becomes rhythm at lower resolution; high-frequency traders see chaos while trend followers appear as scale lengthens because reinforcing impacts add up and short-term zigzags cancel.

claims.speaker: Rich
claims.quote: when you look at the P&L of a convergent system, you get a linear profit
claims.claim: Convergent (mean reversion) strategies earn small linear profits until a negative-skew event causes nonlinear loss; trend following has small linear losses and nonlinear gains from outliers.

claims.speaker: Rich
claims.quote: positive feedback drives reinforcement. Buying therefore attracts more buying
claims.claim: Positive feedback (buying begets buying) moves away from equilibrium and creates trends; negative feedback restores balance; markets oscillate, with quiet periods punctuated by volatility bursts.

claims.speaker: Rich
claims.quote: the frenetic activity that occurs in the shorter time scales are more mean reverting in nature
claims.claim: Shorter time frames are more mean reverting (cancellation) while institutions' interaction at medium to long horizons positively reinforces trends, so one should be a medium-to-long-term trend follower.
claims.direction: trend follow at medium-long horizons; mean-revert short

claims.speaker: Rich
claims.quote: Reversals aren't random. They are feedback inverting
claims.claim: Positive feedback eventually exhausts buyers (valuation stretch, concentration), flips to negative feedback; reversals release stored energy and are fast and violent (gold and metals).

claims.speaker: Rich
claims.quote: trends can actually be a a random result from from um no bias in the price series
claims.claim: Trends can be random, a segment of a mean-reverting cycle, or structural with serial correlation; only the structural kind (outliers) persists, so trends should not be treated as visual patterns.

claims.speaker: Rich
claims.quote: Compression hides structure. Expansion reveals structure
claims.claim: Compression hides structure; expansions are outliers or phase transitions where tails dominate and returns are made.

claims.speaker: Rich
claims.quote: I'm looking for behavioral orthogonality
claims.claim: Diversify trend systems by behavior (breakout, volatility expansion, smooth persistence, mean-reversion into trend) rather than correlation, which is fickle; use ensembles to be ready for any structural form.

claims.speaker: Rich
claims.quote: That's why survival, not expectancy, is the true measure of success
claims.claim: Markets are non-ergodic with one path; ruin ends the game, so survival is the key measure of success including of a manager's track record.

claims.speaker: Rich
claims.quote: So Kelly criterion bad statistic expectancy bad statistic
claims.claim: Rich considers Kelly, expectancy and value-at-risk bad statistics because they derive from a Gaussian model.

claims.speaker: Rich
claims.quote: One experiences losses early and they run out of capital
claims.claim: Identical expectancy gives different outcomes depending on order of wins and losses; -50% then +50% leaves a permanent hole (sequence risk).

claims.speaker: Rich
claims.quote: We use closed balance not floating balance or or equity to size new positions
claims.claim: Size new positions from closed balance (realized capital): it automatically reduces exposure in drawdowns and scales up only after confirmed gains; with positive skew, open equity sits above closed balance so sizing is more conservative.
claims.testable: yes - compare vs full equity sizing

claims.speaker: Rich
claims.quote: a system with uh 5% positive expectancy but have um large size positions
claims.claim: Large position sizes can turn a 5% positive expectancy into ruin through compounding drag; very small positions can make a 2%-expectancy (30% win rate, 3:1) system compound well.

claims.speaker: Niels
claims.quote: it's pretty deal
claims.claim: Niels argues the open equity is not illusory for liquid futures managers who can liquidate in 24 hours, so sizing from full equity is reasonable; closed-balance sizing also reduces volatility like dynamic sizing.

claims.speaker: Niels
claims.quote: only works if you're trading your own capital because you were there at the inception
claims.claim: Closed-balance sizing depends on the inception date; a fund with new client inflows has investors at different entry points, leaving undefined risk for them.

claims.speaker: Niels
claims.quote: a completely discretionary rule um about when you want to cut down your uh position size
claims.claim: The cutback rule is discretionary and also cuts lifting power until a new high; dynamic sizing may increase risk in drawdown, but long-term track records show no big difference in returns.

claims.speaker: Rich
claims.quote: isn't it better just to have the same position size if you're into a big gold trade or into the cocoa trade
claims.claim: Constant position sizing in a big trend (gold, cocoa) may help, but constant sizing in all other positions can detract; both approaches have worked for decades.

claims.speaker: Rich
claims.quote: They view us as a nebulous
claims.claim: Investors should distinguish types of trend follower by objective; varieties differ in philosophy, which is gaining traction among allocators.

claims.speaker: Rich
claims.quote: They're all about crunching data, simulating, abstracting, creating models. But where they lack this ability to define self is they don't contextualize that within the greater environment.
claims.claim: AI models do only the abstract model-building (left-hemisphere) work and lack the feedback loop that checks models against the external environment, so they cannot recalibrate the way a brain does when misaligned (pain, fear).

claims.speaker: Niels
claims.quote: I don't know if it was Ken Griffin or Paul Tuda Jones it seemed like some of those guys who came out and saying well you know
claims.claim: Niels recalls well-known hedge fund managers (possibly Ken Griffin, Paul Tudor Jones) saying AI is far from producing alpha, with gains mainly in programming efficiency rather than alpha production.

claims.speaker: Niels
claims.quote: D A DT for markets. Don't ask, don't think.
claims.claim: Niels reports (his interpretation) that Saxo's former chief strategist links the current private credit debacle to a new market acronym, 'DADT': don't ask, don't think, i.e. investors avoid scrutinising credit risk.

claims.speaker: Niels
claims.quote: I think still people are more biased to looking at the oil price but it hasn't been doing anything for a long time despite all the challenges we've had in um in the Middle East.
claims.claim: Niels notes oil has been largely flat for a long time despite Middle East disruptions, even though most observers still anchor on the oil price rather than electricity as the growth input.
claims.testable: partly - oil price trend history is checkable

claims.speaker: Niels
claims.quote: further sanctions against a couple of oil companies in Russia and the oil prices is up uh quite sharply uh today 5% right now
claims.claim: A policy shock (new US sanctions on Russian oil companies) lifted crude about 5% intraday, an example of an exogenous event that can start an energy trend.

claims.speaker: Niels
claims.quote: Albeit uh there is more volatility in the uh returns from managers um at least when I see the ones I can see on a daily basis uh including our own uh for that matter.
claims.claim: Even in a constructive trend environment, CTA manager returns showed higher day-to-day volatility in late October 2025, linked to big precious metals swings that may mark a short-term top correction.
claims.indicator: manager daily return volatility; precious metals swings
claims.testable: partly - needs CTA index daily data

claims.speaker: Rich
claims.quote: but you just got to stick to the process.
claims.claim: After a poor first six months of 2025 Rich doubted whether the models still worked but argues the discipline is to stick to the process, and that deeper understanding of why trends occur raises his comfort with the methodology.
claims.testable: partly - adherence benefit can be tested vs rule-overriding

claims.speaker: Rich
claims.quote: you know the energies they're turning. They're going bullish. Um the the metals I think you know it might be a bit of a breather for them.
claims.claim: Rich: trend models were turning long in energies while metals might take a breather after their run, but systems remained active in metals (not over yet).
claims.indicator: trend model signals in energies and metals

claims.speaker: Niels
claims.quote: it was only a few years that really were difficult there were also plenty of good years
claims.claim: Caveat: trend following's post-GFC difficulty was limited to a few years (Niels recalls roughly 2018-2020; 2014 was strong), so it was not a decade-long failure.

claims.speaker: Rich
claims.quote: buying the dip syndrome I think was something of the past. I don't think buying the dip is going to continue going forward
claims.claim: Buy-the-dip was a behavioral phenomenon tied to the QE-era compression; with central banks decoupled and markets less correlated, Rich expects it to fade, which favours trends.
claims.conditions: depends on central banks staying uncoordinated
claims.testable: partly - dip-buying payoff and correlations measurable

claims.speaker: Niels
claims.quote: Let me just mention that the trend barometer yesterday finished at 52. So, that is a strong reading and uh it's coming up and uh supports uh what's going on
claims.claim: Niels uses the Trend Barometer (52, rising) as a gauge of how favourable the environment is for trend followers; 52 is read as a strong reading consistent with positive CTA returns.
claims.testable: yes - index series can be tested vs subsequent trend returns

claims.speaker: Niels
claims.quote: traders index up about 1% but still down 4%. Uh so far this year, MSEI World up 40 basis points in October as of last night
claims.claim: SG Short-Term Traders index was about +1% in October but about -4% YTD, much worse than the SG Trend index (+0.53% YTD) and the BTOP50 (+2.58%), i.e. faster-horizon CTAs lagged longer-horizon trend in 2025.
claims.indicator: SG Short-Term Traders index vs SG Trend index

claims.speaker: Rich
claims.quote: that's because liquidity is adaptive. It's not a static pool. It's seen to be like an elastic surface that moves and reforms with order flow.
claims.claim: Liquidity is adaptive, like an elastic surface: each trade consumes liquidity and signals direction, other traders react and quotes adjust, which is why impact is sublinear and the system is nonlinear.

claims.speaker: Rich
claims.quote: the verdict's out whether they are exactly fractal but certainly a fractal model has a better account and can understand why these situations occur
claims.claim: Caveat: Rich does not claim markets are exactly fractal; the fractal market hypothesis is only the closest available account of fat tails and power-law behaviour, not a definitive answer.
claims.testable: partly - tail exponents testable, model choice not decisive

claims.speaker: Rich
claims.quote: then there's um directionless volatility there's directional volatility um one might come with correlation might one might come without correlation
claims.claim: Volatility comes in directionless and directional forms, with or without cross-market correlation; this distinction (rather than a volatility level) is the signature of a live compress-and-expand fractal system.
claims.testable: yes - decomposable via trend vs noise measures

claims.speaker: Rich
claims.quote: I'm not using volatility measures to protect me or statistical measures because I think they're they're unsound.
claims.claim: Rich does not use volatility or other statistical risk measures to protect the portfolio because their assumptions come from a Gaussian world; protection comes from robust system design and sizing instead (the root of his disagreement with volatility-based sizing).
claims.testable: yes - compare drawdown with vol-scaled vs non-scaled sizing

claims.speaker: Rich
claims.quote: But on the hourly chart, those bursts at the micro level appear as clusters. Zoom out to the daily and a narrative forms.
claims.claim: Worked example of feedback cascading across scales (crude oil): tick-level buying ahead of a report, algorithms joining, hourly clusters, a daily narrative, then a monthly systemic move as producers, investors and policymakers reinforce it.

claims.speaker: Rich
claims.quote: Then selling accelerates, stops trigger, the system unwinds. Maybe even margin calls come into play, the system unwinds.
claims.claim: Reversal mechanics: once positive feedback breaks, selling accelerates, stop-losses trigger and margin calls force unwinding, so the energy stored in the trend is released quickly; Rich frames this as system renewal that restarts the cycle (reinforcement, alignment, reversal).
claims.indicator: trend reversals; stops and margin calls
claims.direction: sharp counter-trend moves after extended trends
claims.conditions: after valuation stretch and concentrated positioning
claims.testable: partly - reversal speed vs trend duration testable

claims.speaker: Niels
claims.quote: the risk of this Rich is that you are maybe less classic than than what what other what other trend followers might perceive as being classic
claims.claim: Caveat from Niels: mixing mean-reversion-into-trend and breakout systems in a behaviourally orthogonal ensemble makes Rich's approach less 'classic' trend following than what most allocators expect.

claims.speaker: Rich
claims.quote: We're not trying to forecast variance or optimize volatility. We're simply aligning our capital to the geometry of survival.
claims.claim: Closed-balance sizing aims at avoiding ruin rather than maximising return or targeting volatility; it embeds humility by sizing only from capital that has survived the realized path.
claims.testable: yes - compare terminal wealth and drawdowns under different sizing bases

claims.speaker: Niels
claims.quote: I'm thinking well there must be a reason why the majority at least of managers are not using that methodology.
claims.claim: Niels points out most managers use dynamic (volatility-based) sizing rather than closed-balance sizing, so the two are different design choices, not one right and one wrong; closed-balance sizing also lowers volatility.

claims.speaker: Niels
claims.quote: an easier way to build systems, to understand systems, maybe um maybe with less moving parts, but also a few discretionary parts
claims.claim: Niels concedes closed-balance, trade-by-trade sizing is simpler with fewer moving parts but contains discretionary elements (cutback rule), while dynamic sizing is more complex yet proven over 25-30 years of survival.
